The Tridentine entry ends in 1650. The tie is the synod's own appeal to Trent, not contact with the church of 1517-1650. The Roman authorities of 1720 (the nuncio Grimaldi presided; Benedict XIII confirmed in 1724) belong to the era-8 Catholic ancien-régime entry; I did not draft that pair, since the four fields do not name Rome as an actor.
The professions quote is 'Tridentinam' with the noun 'synodum' on the next, garbled line; the note's wording follows the sense.
That Corpus Christi is a Latin feast is general knowledge, not shown in the quoted lines.
Major judgment: a synod's own law following Trent, counted as a rule changed by an authority. A reviewer may judge it a practice merely taken up.

prose_changes.old: Old Belief is still practiced. Several Old Believer churches exist today — in Russia, Romania, the Baltic states, Alaska, Oregon and South America — some with their own bishops, some with no clergy at all, keeping pre-Nikonian chant, icons and books. Their stubbornness preserved a whole layer of medieval Russian religious culture that the official church had modernized away. Old icon-painting styles, znamenny chant and manuscript practices survived in these communities and were later recovered from them by collectors and scholars. Russian literature never let the schism go either; the raskol runs through the nineteenth-century novel as the standing question of what faithfulness actually costs.
prose_changes.new: Old Belief is still practiced. Old Believer churches exist today in Russia, Romania, the Baltic states, Alaska, Oregon and South America. Some have their own bishops and some have no clergy at all. All keep the chant, icons and books of the time before Nikon. Their stubbornness saved a whole layer of medieval Russian church culture that the official church had modernized away. Old styles of icon painting, znamenny chant and the copying of books by hand lived on in these groups. Collectors and scholars later found them there. Avvakum's own Life, the founding book of the movement, came out in English in 1924.
prose_changes.reason: The closing claim that 'the raskol runs through the nineteenth-century novel' has no source in the library (no Dostoevsky, no Melnikov-Pechersky) and is cut; listed in wants. Replaced by a literary fact the library holds: the Harrison-Mirrlees English Life of 1924 (title page, lines 21-27). The long first sentence is split for reading level; every other fact is kept.

prose_changes.old: The synodal arrangement lasted until 1917, and the church restored the patriarchate almost as soon as the empire fell. The whole shape of modern Russian church-and-state relations was set in this period and is still argued about. Its Alaskan mission planted an Orthodox Christianity that survives among Native communities there to this day, the only Orthodox church established in North America before the nineteenth century. And the tension it created, an official church tied to the state with intense spiritual life running alongside and underneath it, produced both the Optina elders of the following century and the sharp religious searching of Russian literature.
prose_changes.new: The synodal system lasted until 1917, and the church brought back the patriarch almost as soon as the empire fell. The bond between church and state in modern Russia took its shape in this period, and people still argue about it. Its mission to Alaska planted an Orthodox faith that lives on among Native communities there today. It was the only Orthodox church founded in North America before the nineteenth century. The church also lived with a lasting tension. It was an official church tied to the state, with an intense spiritual life running beside and beneath it. The first elders of Optina, in the next century, were trained in this church's own monasteries.
prose_changes.reason: 'Produced ... the sharp religious searching of Russian literature' has no source in the library and is cut (wants). 'The tension it created ... produced the Optina elders' is causal and unshown; restated as what Optina's 1847 preface shows, that Leonid entered Optina in 1797 and served under the bishop of Orel (link russian-church-nikon-to-holy-synod--the-optina-elders-and-russian-ascetic-renewal). The tension itself is kept as the church's condition. The Alaskan sentence is split for reading level; its facts are unchanged and unsourced (see the Alaska link).

prose_changes.old: In 1746 a young monk named Paisius Velichkovsky went looking through the monastery libraries of Mount Athos for old Greek teaching on inward prayer that almost nobody read anymore, and set his community to translating it into Slavonic at Neamț in Moldavia. Printed as the Philokalia at Venice in 1782 and in Paisius's own Slavonic version at Moscow in 1793, that anthology carried a monk's teaching on the Jesus Prayer out to ordinary readers, and fed directly into the elders of Optina and the anonymous classic The Way of a Pilgrim.
prose_changes.new: In 1746 a young monk named Paisius Velichkovsky searched the libraries of the monasteries on Mount Athos. He was looking for old Greek teaching on inward prayer that almost nobody read anymore. At Neamț in Moldavia he set his monks to putting it into Slavonic. The Greek texts were printed as the Philokalia at Venice in 1782. Paisius's own Slavonic version came out at Moscow in 1793. The book carried a monk's teaching on the Jesus Prayer out to ordinary readers. Paisius's own disciples, back in Russia, trained the first of the Optina elders.
prose_changes.reason: 'Fed directly into ... The Way of a Pilgrim' has no source in the library and is cut (wants). 'Fed directly into the elders of Optina' is kept and made exact: Optina's 1847 preface shows Paisius's disciples Theodore and Cleopas training Leonid (link to the Optina elders). Long sentences split for reading level.

prose_changes.old: This is one of the clearest cases anywhere of a book changing a church. The Philokalia is still in print and still read — the standard English translation has been appearing volume by volume since 1979. And the Russian tradition it fed produced the elders of Optina, the anonymous nineteenth-century classic The Way of a Pilgrim, and, through both, the spiritual world of Dostoevsky's novels. Twentieth-century Orthodox theology in the West drew on it heavily, and the Jesus Prayer is now practiced far outside the monasteries the texts were written in. Neamț Monastery still stands and still functions, with Paisius's relics in it; he was canonized in 1988.
prose_changes.new: This is one of the clearest cases anywhere of a book changing a church. The Philokalia is still in print and still read — the standard English translation has been appearing volume by volume since 1979. In Russia it fed the elders of Optina, whose own press printed Paisius's life and writings at Moscow in 1847. The Jesus Prayer is now practiced far outside the monasteries the texts were written in. Neamț Monastery still stands and still functions, with Paisius's relics in it; he was canonized in 1988.
prose_changes.reason: Cut, for want of any source in the library: The Way of a Pilgrim, 'the spiritual world of Dostoevsky's novels', and 'Twentieth-century Orthodox theology in the West drew on it heavily' (all in wants). The Optina claim is kept and grounded in the 1847 Optina edition (title page, line 29-38). Other facts kept as written.
